questions.question: Identify the five igneous intrusions by shape and by their concordant or discordant relationship to the country rock, naming South African examples.
questions.expected_answer: Magma that cools underground forms intrusive igneous rock, classified by size, shape and relationship to the layering of the country rock: concordant intrusions squeeze between the strata, discordant ones cut across them. The batholith is an enormous, deep-seated, discordant granite mass, tens to hundreds of kilometres across with no known floor — the Cape Granite beneath Paarl Mountain and Boulders Beach belongs to such bodies. The laccolith is a smaller concordant intrusion that arched the overlying strata upward into a mushroom-shaped blister with a flat floor and domed roof. The lopolith is a huge concordant saucer whose weight sagged the strata beneath it — the Bushveld Igneous Complex north of Pretoria is the world's largest and holds most of the planet's platinum. The dyke is a discordant vertical or near-vertical wall of magma frozen in a crack, cutting the strata; the sill is its concordant twin, a near-horizontal sheet between strata, exemplified by the Karoo dolerite sills that cap the mesas and buttes.

questions.question: Explain how granite domes form, covering pressure release, sheet jointing and exfoliation, and why the dome becomes more rounded as it erodes.
questions.expected_answer: Granite that crystallised kilometres underground did so under the pressure of the overlying rock. As erosion strips that overburden, the pressure drops and the granite expands slightly — pressure release or unloading. The expansion cracks the rock in curved sheet joints parallel to the land surface, wrapped around the mass like onion layers. Weathering then exploits the joints: water enters them, heating and cooling flex the outer sheets, and the curved slabs loosen and peel away — exfoliation. Because the sheets are curved, each one that is shed exposes a fresh, smoother, more rounded surface beneath, so the dome renews and perfects its own curvature as it wastes rather than crumbling. The result is a bare, smooth exfoliation dome — a large isolated example over a plain is a bornhardt — with Paarl Mountain's granite domes as the South African textbook case and the whalebacked Matopos hills as the regional one.

questions.question: Describe the two-stage formation of tors, the role of joints and joint spacing, and how erosion converts each buried intrusion into a distinctive surface landform.
questions.expected_answer: Stage one happens underground: granite is divided by roughly vertical and horizontal joints into rectangular blocks, and water seeping along the joints drives chemical weathering inward from every crack. Corners are attacked from three sides and decay fastest, edges from two, faces slowest, so each block rounds into a hard corestone wrapped in rotted, crumbly granite called grus. Stage two is exhumation: erosion strips the soft grus and leaves the corestones freestanding, stacked in their original joint-given positions, as a tor. Joint spacing decides the outcome — widely spaced joints leave huge blocks that weather into domes, closely spaced joints produce corestones and tors, so one koppie can carry both. More broadly, intrusions become landforms when erosion strips their cover and the resistant igneous rock stands while the country rock wastes: batholiths emerge as massive rounded granite mountain and dome landscapes, laccoliths as granite-cored dome hills, the Bushveld lopolith as a broad basin-like region announced by its platinum and chrome mines, resistant dykes as straight wall-like ridges ignoring the drainage — or trenches where the dyke is softer — and resistant sills as level cliff bands, mesa caps and waterfall lips such as the escarpment edges over which the Drakensberg rivers fall.
